entities.summary:
The Battle of Poitiers, fought on September 19, 1356, was a pivotal clash between the English and French armies in the Hundred Years' War, marking a decisive English victory that would shape the course of European history.

The battle took place in Nouaillé-Maupertuis, a small village in western France, where the English army, led by the Black Prince, Edward of Woodstock, deployed clever tactics to outmaneuver the French forces, led by King John II. The English longbowmen played a crucial role in the battle, raining arrows on the French knights and infantry, causing heavy casualties.

The outcome of the Battle of Poitiers had far-reaching consequences. King John II was captured by the English, and the French army was severely defeated, leading to a significant shift in the balance of power in Western Europe. The English victory at Poitiers marked the beginning of a period of English dominance in France, which would last for several decades.

The Battle of Poitiers has left an indelible mark on the history of warfare. It showcased the effectiveness of the longbow on the battlefield, an innovation that would influence military tactics for centuries to come. The battle also highlighted the importance of mobility and adaptability in warfare, as the English army demonstrated its ability to pivot and respond to changing circumstances on the battlefield.
